title: Complete the J1 command path: graph activation and final acceptance
description:
Objective: expose the goal and graph commands the core already implements as authenticated durable daemon handlers, so J1's three human actions are drivable end to end. Created by architect-0b81de40 2026-08-09 from the Foundation canary's block report, verified symbol by symbol on disk. THIS IS THE M1 EXIT BLOCKER: the epic's exit condition is that J1, J3 and J4 pass, and J1 currently cannot complete.

THE GAP, MEASURED 2026-08-09. Design line 1095 defines J1's per-goal happy path as exactly three human actions: (1) goal.create, (2) exact plan/initial-graph approval, (3) final acceptance of the verified/reviewed result. On disk:
  apps/daemon/src/goals/goal-services.ts:66   GOAL_HANDLERS = { "goal.create": createGoal }        <- action 1 only
  apps/daemon/src/planning/planning-services.ts:156  PLANNING_HANDLERS = { "approval.decide", "plan.propose" }
  BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND_KINDS (9 total): approval.decide, goal.create, plan.propose, policy.install, policy.validate, project.activate, project.bind_repository, project.register, provider.probe
There is NO final-acceptance command and NO goal.close anywhere in the daemon, and approval.decide records a generic approval without activating the graph. So action 3 is entirely absent and action 2 is incomplete.

THIS IS COMPOSITION, NOT NEW DOMAIN LOGIC - which is what makes it a bounded task. @moe/core ALREADY implements everything needed, verified on disk:
  packages/core/src/goal/goal-contract.ts - GoalActivateInitialGraphCommand (:71), GoalCloseCommand (:76), GoalCancelCommand (:87), GoalQualificationInvalidatedCommand (:82), GoalReopenAsRevisionCommand (:92), GoalPauseCommand, GoalResumeCommand, and the GoalCommand union (:111)
  packages/core/src/goal/goal-reducer.ts - reduceGoal, GOAL_COMMAND_KINDS, GOAL_TRANSITIONS, plus validators validActivation, validClosure, validCancellation, validInvalidation, validExpectedVersion, validProjectReady
  packages/core/src/planning/planning-command-contract.ts - PlanApprovalWitness (:112), PlanningActivationWitness (:117), PlanRevisionSeal (:102), SubmissionFinalizeWitness (:86)
The daemon exposes handlers for two of the goal commands' worth of surface while the core implements eight. The witnesses for activation and approval exist and are unused.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT ON ACTION 2, do not simplify it away. Design line 299 states that J1's one approval action commits plan and graph decisions PLUS activation atomically - one human click, one transaction. Recording an approval and activating the graph in two separate commands would break J1's three-action contract and is not what the design describes.

Deliverable: daemon handlers for initial-graph activation (composed into the existing approval command so it stays ONE action) and for final acceptance plus goal closure, each following the daemon's established shape - bounded decode, exact-shape gate against a frozen key list with a pinned schemaVersion, reduce through the core, commit the verdict durably through the store, return a frozen discriminated result. The services compose; they never decide.

NOT in scope: new domain rules in @moe/core (it is frozen contract per M4-style rails and already complete); J3 launcher/restart composition; J4 review persistence; the review flow itself; any HTTP or transport change.

Hard dependencies: none - every consumed symbol is committed at HEAD.

Owned paths: apps/daemon/src/goals/**, apps/daemon/src/planning/**, and apps/daemon/src/bootstrap/bootstrap-contracts.ts (command-kind vocabulary only).
Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test && pnpm typecheck
definitionOfDone: J1's three human actions are each drivable through the published @moe/daemon root with no deep subpath import: goal.create, ONE approval action that atomically commits the plan/graph decision AND activates the initial graph (design line 299 - not two separate commands), and a final acceptance of the verified reviewed result. A test drives all three in sequence against the real store and asserts the goal reaches its accepted terminal state.

Every new handler composes rather than decides: it reduces through @moe/core's reduceGoal or the planning contract and commits the reducer's verdict, and a rejected reducer result is surfaced with the CORE's own reason code rather than a locally invented one, so which layer refused survives. Asserted by feeding a command the core rejects and pinning that exact code.

Final acceptance is evidence-bound and cannot be forged: acceptance requires the verification and review witnesses the core's validators demand, and an acceptance attempted without them refuses with its specific stable code and commits NOTHING - proven by reading the store back, not by the returned value, since a service that mutates then refuses would pass a return-value-only assertion.

Activation is atomic with approval: an approval whose activation half fails leaves NEITHER committed, proven by fault injection rather than by inspection. A partially-applied approval is the defect this DoD exists to catch.

Each command is idempotent on replay: issuing it twice returns the same terminal decision and leaves exactly one durable row, asserted by reading the row count back rather than by the second call not throwing.

The command-kind vocabulary is extended, not forked: the new kinds are appended to BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND_KINDS and the handler tables, and a set-equality assertion pins the full kind list so an unreviewed command cannot appear unnoticed.
pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test && pnpm typecheck all exit 0, and only owned paths are staged and committed by explicit pathspec.
taskRails: Compose, never decide. Every rule lives in @moe/core already; a daemon handler that re-implements a validation the core owns creates a second source of truth that will drift. If a needed rule seems missing from the core, report_blocked rather than inventing it here.

Design line 299 is binding: J1's approval is ONE human action that commits plan and graph decisions plus activation atomically. Do not split it into approve-then-activate to make implementation easier - that changes the product contract the epic's exit condition is written against.

Assert the reason code AND the refusing layer. Both the daemon's shape gate and a core validator can refuse the same command; a test asserting only 'refused' would stay green if the shape gate started answering first.
Prove non-mutation by reading the store back, never by trusting a returned value. A service that mutates and then refuses passes a return-value-only assertion.
Extend the frozen vocabularies by APPENDING; never reorder or remove an entry, since existing suites assert against those arrays.
No new .js bridge convention decisions here - apps/daemon now has bridges, so any new module needs its sibling bridge in the same commit, one line, LF, trailing newline.
Keep each production source focused, target <=250 lines, split before 400. Commit by explicit pathspec only; several agents share this working directory.

Then WRITE DOWN, by hand from design lines 1095 and 299, the exact mapping from J1's three human actions to the command set you will implement — in particular which single command carries both the plan/graph decision and activation. Read `bootstrap-services.ts:48` for the established handler shape ('reduce, then commit only on acceptance') and copy it rather than inventing a second idiom. KEY CONSTRAINT FOUND, drives the design: the store's decision seam commits ONE targetAggregateId per decision (store-contracts.ts:74-84), so "atomic" here means one commitExpectedVersionDecision call. The approval+activation pair therefore targets the GOAL aggregate with result = exact GoalState (snapshotGoalState/validGoalState require exactly the 12 state keys, so the result cannot be a wrapper), and the decided approval record rides in the committed EVENT payload - durable and readable via store.readEvents(goalId). implementationPlan.description: TDD red for the atomic approval-plus-activation action — J1's second human action and design line 299. Extend the planning suite before touching the handler. Assert: a single approval command commits the plan/graph decision AND activates the initial graph, leaving the goal in its activated state after ONE call, not two; the activation is reduced through the core's GoalActivateInitialGraphCommand path and its verdict is what gets committed, with the core's own reason code surfaced verbatim on rejection rather than a locally invented one; and THE ATOMICITY CASE, which is the defect most likely to ship silently — force the activation half to fail and assert NEITHER the approval nor the activation is durable, read back from the store rather than inferred from the return value. An approval that lands without its activation leaves the goal in a state J1 has no action to escape, so this assertion is the point of the step. Also assert the refusing LAYER wherever both the daemon's shape gate and a core validator could answer. Red.
implementationPlan.note:
RED confirmed: `pnpm exec vitest run --root . --config package.json src/planning` -> "Tests 7 failed | 8 passed (15)", 1 file failed. The 7 reds are exactly the new atomic approval-plus-activation arms.

New describe block "approval activates the initial graph atomically (design 299)" carries seven arms, each reading the store back rather than trusting the returned value:
1. ONE call leaves the goal EXECUTION_ENABLED with activeGraphRevisionRef/graphEpoch 1/version 2 AND decisionCount +1 exactly - the "+1" is what proves it was not two commands.
2. The committed activation's graphApprovalRef equals the core's own decided approvalRef, read out of the durable event ledger - an activation cannot name an approval that was not the one just decided.
3. ATOMICITY, activation half fails (activation.truthClass SELF_REPORTED so the core's validActivation is the layer that answers): CORE_REDUCER/ILLEGAL_TRANSITION, decisionCount unchanged, goal still DRAFT, no approval evidence in the goal's events, ledger.kinds has no approval.decide.
4. ATOMICITY, stale expectedGoalVersion: CORE_REDUCER/EXPECTED_VERSION_CONFLICT, neither half durable.
5. ATOMICITY, approval half fails (stepUpAuthRef null) while the activation evidence is valid: goal still DRAFT with activeGraphRevisionRef null - the activation must not land on its own.
6. Missing activation half: DAEMON_INGRESS/BOOTSTRAP_PAYLOAD_INVALID (the shape gate, distinct from the core arms above).
7. A REJECT decision cannot activate a graph: DAEMON_PREREQUISITE/BOOTSTRAP_PAYLOAD_INVALID, nothing durable.

Layer is asserted on every refusal arm, since the shape gate, the daemon revision gate and the core reducer can all answer here.

Test helper `durableApprovalRefs` decodes the goal aggregate's stored event payloads via store.readEvents - the non-mutation assertions therefore read durable bytes, not the response.

Fixtures added to bootstrap-test-fixtures.ts: GRAPH_REVISION_REF, planningActivation() (core PlanningActivationWitness), approvalPayload(), closureWitness(), zeroAuthorityWitness(), acceptancePayload(); bootstrapSequence() now carries the approval via approvalPayload() and appends the tenth entry envelope("goal.close", 2, acceptancePayload()).

implementationPlan.description: Implement the atomic approval-plus-activation handler to green in apps/daemon/src/planning/planning-services.ts. Compose the existing approval decision with the core's initial-graph activation inside ONE store transaction, so the pair is all-or-nothing. Do NOT introduce a separate `graph.activate` command to make this easier: design line 299 makes this one human action and design 1095 counts exactly three actions per goal, so splitting it would change the journey the epic's exit condition is measured against — if it proves genuinely hard, report that as a finding rather than splitting. The handler composes and never decides: it hands the parsed command to reduceGoal and the planning contract, commits the reducer's verdict through the store's expected-version decision seam, and surfaces a rejection with the core's reason code. Bind the approval and activation witnesses (PlanApprovalWitness, PlanningActivationWitness) that the core already defines rather than inventing new evidence shapes. Keep the file under 250 lines; split before 400, and give any new module its sibling `.js` bridge in the same commit, since apps/daemon is now covered by the repo-wide runtime-loadability gate.
implementationPlan.note:
GREEN: src/planning 15/15 passing, `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck` exit 0. planning-services.ts 183 lines, approval-activation.ts 83 lines - both under the 250 target. Sibling .js bridge created in the same change (one line, LF, trailing newline) since apps/daemon is covered by the runtime-loadability gate.

No `graph.activate` command was introduced: the activation composes INSIDE approval.decide, so J1 stays at three human actions.

HOW ATOMICITY IS ACHIEVED, and the constraint that forced it. The store commits ONE targetAggregateId per decision (store-contracts.ts:74-84), so "one transaction" here means one commitExpectedVersionDecision call carrying both halves. `decideApproval` performs NO commit of its own - every gate returns early and the single commit happens in `activateInitialGraph`, so a partial approval is not merely rejected but unrepresentable. The decision targets the GOAL aggregate because that is the lifecycle J1's third action must read back; the committed result is a bare GoalState (snapshotGoalState/validGoalState accept exactly the twelve state keys, so a wrapper would make the goal unreadable to goal.close) and the decided approval record rides in the same decision's EVENT payload, which is what the tests read back.

COMPOSES, NEVER DECIDES. The InitialGraphActivationWitness is assembled, not accepted: graphApprovalRef is the CORE's own decided approvalRef (never a payload field), so an activation cannot cite an approval other than the one just decided; activeGraphRevisionRef is the payload ref; truthClass comes from the caller's PlanningActivationWitness so the core's strongTruth check stays load-bearing and reachable. expectedVersion is the witness's own expectedGoalVersion, judged by the core's validExpectedVersion and version check. goalRef is read from the DURABLE run state, not the request, so an activation cannot be redirected at a goal this plan was never proposed for. Every rejection returns refuseFromCore, i.e. the core's code verbatim under CORE_REDUCER.

ONE daemon-layer judgement was added beyond the existing revision-hash gate: a decision that is not APPROVE cannot carry an activation (DAEMON_PREREQUISITE/BOOTSTRAP_PAYLOAD_INVALID, an existing published code - no new code invented). Without it a REJECT would activate the graph the human refused. Consequence to record: a typed decline is NOT expressible on this surface; that is J4's journey and separately owned.

FINDING, reported rather than worked around per the step's instruction. The core ALREADY implements design 299 fully as reducePlanningRun's `graph.approve` (planning-run-submission.ts:138, comment "J1: plan decision, graph decision, and activation commit as one atomic result"), which consumes PlanApprovalWitness + PlanningActivationWitness and drives the run to ACTIVATED. I did NOT fold it in, so the planning RUN's lifecycle does not advance on approval. Two reasons: (a) it needs the run in PLAN_REVIEW, which needs planning.finalize_submission, which the existing plan.propose handler forbids as a chain tail (planning-services.ts requires the last chain command to be plan.propose); (b) it would make a THIRD aggregate part of the same decision, which the single-aggregate decision seam cannot do atomically without changing bootstrap-ledger.ts - outside this task's owned paths and shared with sibling tasks. The pair this task's plan names (approval decision + goal initial-graph activation) IS atomic. Folding the planning-run half is a follow-up.

implementationPlan.description: TDD red for final acceptance and goal closure — J1's third human action, which is entirely absent today and is the highest-risk handler in this task. Extend the goals suite. Assert the happy path: a verified and reviewed result can be accepted, driving the goal to its accepted terminal state through the core's validClosure path. Then the assertions that matter more, because acceptance is what turns work into an accepted terminal state and a forged acceptance is the worst defect available here: an acceptance attempted WITHOUT the verification and review witnesses the core's validators demand must refuse with its specific stable code AND commit nothing — prove the non-mutation by reading the store back, since a handler that mutates and then refuses passes a return-value-only assertion; an acceptance against a goal in a state the core's transition table does not admit refuses with the core's own code; and an acceptance carrying a stale expected version is refused by validExpectedVersion rather than silently overwriting. Assert the refusing layer on each, since the daemon's shape gate and a core validator can both answer. Red.
implementationPlan.note:
RED confirmed: `pnpm exec vitest run --root . --config package.json src/goals` -> "Tests 8 failed | 4 passed (12)". The 8 reds are the new acceptance arms plus the handler-table assertion.

New describe "goal close accepts the verified result", seven arms; every refusal arm reads the goal row back out of readDurableLedger rather than trusting the returned value:
1. Happy path: goal reaches COMPLETED (accepted terminal) in ONE decision, version 2 -> 4 because the core's `close` emits GoalClosing AND GoalCompleted from one command, and activeGraphRevisionRef returns to null.
2. No closureWitness: DAEMON_INGRESS/BOOTSTRAP_PAYLOAD_INVALID, decisionCount unchanged, goal still EXECUTION_ENABLED.
3. No zeroAuthorityWitness: DAEMON_INGRESS/BOOTSTRAP_PAYLOAD_INVALID, and the goal is asserted NOT to be CLOSING. This is the arm that keeps J1 at three actions - the core's `close` with only the closure witness parks the goal in CLOSING, which J1 has no fourth action to escape, so requiring both witnesses is what makes acceptance one action.
4. closureWitness with noPendingDraftOrSupersession false: shaped enough to pass the daemon gate, so CORE_REDUCER/ILLEGAL_TRANSITION via validClosure is what answers. Nothing durable.
5. closureWitness with truthClass SELF_REPORTED: CORE_REDUCER/ILLEGAL_TRANSITION via strongTruth. Nothing durable.
6. Stale expectedVersion 99: CORE_REDUCER/EXPECTED_VERSION_CONFLICT, nothing durable, no silent overwrite.
7. Second acceptance of an already COMPLETED goal with a DISTINCT commandId so the replay path cannot answer: CORE_REDUCER/ILLEGAL_TRANSITION from the transition table, version still 4.

Layer is pinned on every arm: arms 2-3 name DAEMON_INGRESS, arms 4-7 name CORE_REDUCER, so a shape gate that started answering first would redden the core arms instead of silently satisfying them.

implementationPlan.description: Implement final acceptance and goal closure to green in apps/daemon/src/goals/goal-services.ts, extending GOAL_HANDLERS. Follow the same shape as createGoal and the bootstrap services: bounded decode, exact-shape gate against a frozen key list with a pinned schemaVersion, reduce through reduceGoal using the core's GoalCloseCommand and its neighbours, commit only on acceptance, return a frozen discriminated result. The acceptance path is evidence-bound BY CONSTRUCTION where possible — require the witness fields the core's validators consume, so an acceptance without evidence is not merely rejected but hard to express — with the stable refusal code as the backstop. Surface the core's reason code verbatim on rejection; a locally invented code would erase which layer refused and would drift from the core's rules. Append the new kinds to BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND_KINDS and to GOAL_HANDLERS rather than reordering either, since existing suites assert against those arrays.
implementationPlan.note:
GREEN: full daemon suite `pnpm exec vitest run --root . --config package.json src` -> "Test Files 16 passed (16) / Tests 382 passed (382)".

`closeGoal` follows createGoal's shape exactly: payload accessors, refuse at DAEMON_INGRESS on shape, reduce through reduceGoal with the core's GoalCloseCommand, refuseFromCore verbatim on rejection, commit only on acceptance via the one durable seam. goal-services.ts is 114 lines.

EVIDENCE-BOUND BY CONSTRUCTION: both closureWitness and zeroAuthorityWitness are required by the shape gate. The reason is structural, not a judgement the daemon is making - the core's `close` moves a goal carrying only the closure witness to CLOSING, and a goal parked mid-closure has no fourth J1 action to escape. The core remains the only layer that decides whether either witness HOLDS (validClosure/validZeroAuthority/strongTruth), and its code is surfaced unchanged.

implementationPlan.description: Drive J1 end to end and prove replay idempotence — DoD 1 and DoD 5. Add a test that runs all three human actions in sequence against the REAL store through the published @moe/daemon root, with no deep subpath import: goal.create, then the single approval-plus-activation action, then final acceptance of the verified reviewed result — asserting the goal reaches its accepted terminal state and that exactly three human actions were required, since a fourth would mean J1's contract was broken by the implementation. Then idempotence for EACH command: issue it twice with the identical request and assert the second returns the same terminal decision AND that the durable row count is still one, read back from the store. The row-count assertion is the load-bearing half — 'it did not throw the second time' is exactly what a double write also looks like. Finally assert the command-kind vocabulary by SET EQUALITY against a hand-written list so an unreviewed command kind cannot appear unnoticed, and assert the generated case count is non-zero.
implementationPlan.note:
New file apps/daemon/src/goals/j1-command-path.test.ts, 15 tests, all green (`src/goals` -> 2 files, 27 passed). Every PRODUCTION symbol is imported from the published `@moe/daemon` root via `import * as daemon` - runBootstrapCommand, BOOTSTRAP_HANDLERS, GOAL_HANDLERS, PLANNING_HANDLERS, BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND_KINDS, HandlerTable, ServiceOutcome. No deep subpath import. The fixtures supply request DATA only.

DoD 1, three human actions: the journey drives bootstrapSequence() in order through the root pipeline against a real SqliteEventStore and counts the entries whose kind is one of the hand-restated ["goal.create","approval.decide","goal.close"]. It asserts the counted kinds EQUAL that list in order, that there are exactly 3, and that the goal is already COMPLETED at the moment the third one returns - so a fourth action is provably never needed. A second arm walks to just before goal.close and asserts DRAFT after goal.create and EXECUTION_ENABLED after the single approval, which is what pins the activation as being INSIDE the approval rather than a separate action.

`daemon.readDurableLedger` is NOT a package-root export, so lifecycle is decoded from the store's own committed decision rows (resultBytes of the latest EFFECTS_COMMITTED decision targeting the goal). That keeps the journey honest as an external-consumer proof rather than reaching into daemon internals.

DoD 5, idempotence: it.each over all ten sequence entries. Each sends the identical request twice and asserts DECIDED then REPLAYED, identical decisionId and resultSha256, AND `rowsFor(store, commandId) === 1` both times - counted by scanning store.readCommandDecisionsAfter, not inferred from the response, since "it did not throw" is exactly what a double write also looks like.

DoD 6, vocabulary: set equality of daemon.BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND_KINDS against a 10-entry literal restated BY HAND in this file, independently of bootstrap-services.test.ts, plus both length pins. A second arm asserts the merged root handler table's key set equals the same literal, so a published kind with no handler (or a handler with no kind) reddens.

implementationPlan.description: Prove the guards are load-bearing, then run the gates. MUTATION DRILL at each mechanism's single source: the acceptance evidence requirement, the expected-version check pass-through, the transaction boundary that makes approval and activation atomic, and the exact-shape key list. Neutralise each operand with a constant — NEVER delete a line, since a deleted line from a multi-line condition is a syntax error that reddens the suite for the wrong reason. Count failed SUITES as well as failed tests, and confirm the red test is the one naming that guard's code. The transaction-boundary mutation is the one to watch: if removing the shared transaction leaves the suite green, DoD 4's atomicity is untested regardless of how the suite looks. This worktree is shared and another agent's completion hook can commit your mutation, so capture `git rev-parse HEAD:<path>` before each drill and verify the restore against that sha rather than `git status`. Then run fresh: pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test && pnpm typecheck, all exiting 0. - Approval without activation? Structurally impossible: decideApproval performs no commit at all; the single commitExpectedVersionDecision lives in activateInitialGraph after reduceGoal accepts. Drill C (approval committed separately first) reddened 4 suites / 19 tests.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
(1) ONE APPROVAL ACTION, NOT TWO. The easy implementation is `approval.decide` records the decision and a new `graph.activate` follows. I am ruling that out and the rail says so: design line 299 states J1's one approval action commits plan and graph decisions PLUS activation atomically, and design 1095 counts exactly three human actions per goal. Splitting it would make J1 a four-action journey and quietly change the product contract the epic's exit condition is written against. Activation composes INTO the existing approval handler, in one transaction.
(2) THE SCOPE IS COMPOSITION, WHICH IS WHY THIS FITS ONE TASK. @moe/core already implements every rule: eight goal commands with their validators, and the planning approval/activation witnesses. The daemon exposes handlers covering two of them. Nothing here needs new domain logic, which is what keeps a task touching the epic's exit gate down to a handful of files.
(3) ACCEPTANCE IS THE RISKIEST HANDLER and gets the most assertion weight. It is the one command that turns work into an accepted terminal state, so a forged or evidence-free acceptance is the worst possible defect in this task. It must be evidence-bound through the core's validators, and the test must read the store back rather than trusting a return value.
(4) I did NOT bundle J3 (launcher/restart composition) or J4 (review persistence), which the canary also names as missing. They are separate journeys with separate surfaces, and bundling them would blow both the step and file caps and make the exit gate depend on one oversized task.

planningNotes.risks:
1. **The atomicity of approval+activation is the defect most likely to ship silently.** If the two writes are not in one transaction, an approval whose activation half fails leaves the goal approved-but-not-activated — a state J1 has no action to escape. Prove it by fault injection, not by reading the code: force the activation write to fail and assert NEITHER half is durable.
2. **A forged acceptance is the worst outcome in this task.** Acceptance turns work into an accepted terminal state, so it must be evidence-bound through the core's validators and must refuse without them. Assert the refusal code AND read the store back — a handler that mutates then refuses passes a return-value-only assertion.
3. **Do not let the daemon re-implement a core rule.** Both layers can refuse the same command; if a handler restates a validation the core owns, the two drift and epic rail 6's 'assert against the production surface' is violated by construction. Surface the CORE's reason code verbatim.
4. **Extend the frozen vocabularies by appending only.** Existing suites assert against BOOTSTRAP_COMMAND_KINDS and the handler tables; a reorder or removal breaks a foreign green suite and reads as your regression.
5. **Resist the four-action shortcut.** If activation inside approval proves genuinely hard, that is a finding to report, not a licence to split the command — splitting changes the journey the epic's exit is measured against.
6. **`apps/daemon` is now covered by the runtime-loadability gate**, so a new module without its `.js` bridge will fail that gate rather than passing quietly as it would have last week.
7. This task does NOT unblock the canary by itself — J3 (launcher/restart composition) and J4 (review persistence) remain missing and are separately owned. Say so in the completion evidence so nobody reads a green J1 as a green canary.
